opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be here.

The way I think about it, trustworthy AI comes down to a fairly simple question: when can we rely on these systems, and how would we know? That splits our work into a few connected threads.

The first is measurement. A lot of what we say about AI systems, that a model is fair, robust, or capable of some kind of reasoning, rests on evaluations that are often shakier than people realize. So we spend a lot of time on the science of evaluation. What does a benchmark actually measure? How do we build metrics that capture what we care about? When we see something like an "emergent capability," is it a real change in the model, or partly an artifact of how we chose to score it? I think getting measurement right is the foundation. If you can't measure trustworthiness reliably, you can't really improve it.

The second thread is the properties themselves: fairness, robustness, privacy, and reliability under distribution shift. We approach these with a mix of theory and practice. We ask what guarantees are achievable, what the fundamental tradeoffs are, and then how to build methods that hold up in real deployments rather than only in clean lab settings.

The third thread, which matters a lot to me personally, is grounding all of this in real applications, especially in health and the sciences. Those settings have real stakes, the data is messy, and the people affected aren't always the ones designing the system. They force you to be honest about whether your notions of trust actually mean anything.

Running through all of it is a sociotechnical view. Trustworthiness isn't purely a property of the model. It depends on who is using the system, for what purpose, and in what context. So we try to keep the technical work connected to the human and institutional side: who gets to define what "good" looks like, and who bears the cost when the system gets it wrong.

In short: measure carefully, understand the properties deeply, and stay grounded in the places where this actually matters.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluation and measurement, then studying trustworthiness properties and building methods for deployment. It does not clearly distinguish assessing trustworthiness gaps from developing mitigations to close those gaps.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I usually frame it is that trustworthy AI isn't one problem, it's a cluster of properties we want systems to have before we're comfortable deploying them in settings that matter. In my lab we've organized that around a few pillars: robustness, fairness, privacy, and more recently things like calibration and interpretability. And the honest framing is that these aren't independent. A lot of our work ends up living at the intersections, where you discover that improving one property has consequences for another.

So a question we ask a lot is, what does it actually mean to measure trustworthiness? Benchmarks are a big part of that for us. If you can't measure a property rigorously, you can't claim you've improved it, and you definitely can't make guarantees about it. That's what motivated projects like DecodingTrust, where we tried to systematically evaluate large language models across toxicity, stereotype bias, adversarial robustness, privacy leakage, and so on, rather than looking at any one dimension in isolation.

The second thread is more foundational, coming out of my background in statistical machine learning. There I'm interested in the theory behind these properties: when can you guarantee a model will be robust to distribution shift, what's the right formalization of fairness for a given task, where are the fundamental tradeoffs. Theory and measurement feed each other. Theory tells you what to look for, and the empirical side keeps you honest about whether the assumptions hold in practice.

And the third thread, which has become increasingly central, is grounding all of this in application domains, especially healthcare and neuroscience. Those settings force you to be concrete. A fairness definition that looks elegant on paper can be meaningless or even harmful when you talk to clinicians about how a model would actually be used. So we try to keep that loop tight, letting real deployment questions shape which problems we think are worth solving.

r001.rationale: The response describes evaluating trustworthiness through benchmarks and developing theory, but it does not clearly distinguish gap assessment from developing mitigations to close those gaps in deployed systems.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is: how do we build machine learning systems that we can trust to do what we want them to do? Accuracy is part of that, but it’s not the whole story. We also care about things like fairness, robustness, privacy, and understanding when a model might fail.

One of the interesting research challenges is making those goals precise. What does fairness mean in a particular application? What kinds of changes in the environment should a system be robust to? And how do we evaluate whether we’ve actually achieved those properties?

So the agenda connects those foundational questions to developing algorithms and evaluating systems in context. The goal is to understand what guarantees we can provide, what tradeoffs we’re making, and where the limits are.

r001.rationale: The response mentions evaluating system properties and developing algorithms, but does not clearly distinguish assessing trustworthiness gaps from creating mitigations to close those gaps in deployed systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to frame it around a fairly simple question: how do we build machine learning systems that people can actually trust? And that means going beyond asking whether a model has good average accuracy. We also need to ask where it fails, who those failures affect, and whether we can understand and manage those failures.

So that brings together questions about fairness, robustness, privacy, and uncertainty. We’re interested in the mathematical foundations of those properties, but also in how you measure them and build them into practical systems. Often there are tradeoffs, and part of the research is making those tradeoffs explicit rather than assuming there’s one definition of trustworthy AI that works in every setting.

r001.rationale: The response mentions identifying and measuring failures, then building trustworthiness properties into practical systems, but it does not clearly distinguish assessing gaps from developing mitigations to close them in deployed systems.
